abstract: Domestic connectivity via passenger transport infrastructure can affect a country’s exports by easing information frictions. We study this mechanism using China’s high-speed rail network, which connects cities to same-sector exporters in other cities without directly affecting freight costs. Stronger connections increase firms’ export sales and expand both destination and product scope, with no change in domestic sales, total employment, or shipping costs. The effects are largest for firms facing greater information barriers. Connected firms upgrade product quality and their export destinations converge toward those of newly connected peers, with initially weaker firms converging toward stronger connected peers while stronger firms show little adjustment. A within-firm cross-destination specification confirms that improved connectivity generates destination-specific benefits. The results point to an information-based channel through which passenger connectivity affects trade, including knowledge about export markets and inputs.

abstract: Europe's energy transition is increasingly shaped by geopolitical competition, strategic dependence and investment uncertainty. This conceptual paper develops the concept of geopolitical sequencing to explain how geopolitical pressures interact with strategic infrastructure, political legitimacy and transition finance. The central argument is temporal: political commitments, infrastructure development and financing arrangements evolve at different speeds, generating misalignment between strategic ambitions and implementation capacity. Institutional risk compression is introduced as the governance mechanism through which socio-political durability, regulatory credibility and financial arrangements interact to contain or amplify uncertainty. The framework is explored through a case study of Sicily, a strategic Mediterranean energy node connecting North African gas corridors, renewable development, grid interconnections and prospective EU–Africa energy partnerships. Evidence on infrastructure investment, renewable permitting and cross-border financing illustrates how geopolitical priorities interact with territorial distributional tensions, regulatory constraints and investment conditions. The analysis highlights three interconnected challenges: aligning commitments across different time horizons, reconciling system-wide infrastructure benefits with local legitimacy and distinguishing genuine risk reduction from the redistribution of financial exposure. The paper contributes a framework for understanding how geopolitical pressures are transmitted through regional energy transitions and identifies implications for EU energy security, infrastructure governance and transition finance.
title: Geopolitical sequencing in Europe's energy transition: infrastructure, legitimacy and finance

abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. We also find that unconditional model rankings closely mirror those in bull markets, overstating the superiority of the models identified as best performing in expansions by ignoring the performance convergence across models that emerges in downturns. This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04942 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching

abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: K. J. Mitchener thanks the Ciocca Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation at Santa Clara University for funding this research (Grant 2024-CIOG11). Any views expressed in this paper exclusively represent those of the authors and do not reflect the official viewpoint of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, the European Central Bank, or the Eurosystem. title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand

abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01302 .

title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand

abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge support from the FRIC Center for Financial Frictions [Grant DNRF102]. title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices

abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08298 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data

abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09021 .

title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem

abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we caution that a more efficient waste valorization process may lead to negative outcomes for both the manufacturer and the environment. This analysis not only sheds light on how waste valorization contributes to waste reduction and economic value, but also provides insights for production decision making. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Financial support from the National Science Foundation of China [Grants 72301055, 72322017, 72471244, and 72101102] is gratefully acknowledged. abstract: In recent years, military power has re-emerged as a central driver of international economic relations. Economic theories have largely dismissed militarism as irrational rent-seeking that distorts markets or they have focused predominantly on its impact on domestic economic performance. Both these perspectives, however, overlook the mutually reinforcing dynamic between military power and the reproduction of global economic asymmetries. Instead, this paper introduces what we term the imperialist feedback loop, which operates as follows: the technological and financial dominance of core economies provides the foundation for military dominance, which is then instrumental to reproduce the asymmetric global division of labour underpinning technological and financial dominance itself. Empirically, we employ a hidden Markov model to dynamically cluster country panel data (1988–2023), identifying a stable hierarchical world structure, wherein the stability of the imperialist core is tied to the existence of an impoverished periphery and limited upward mobility from the semi-periphery. The empirical validation of militarism’s core role in reproducing imperialist structures can inform the design of policies aimed at counteracting the technological-military dependency of less-developed countries, ultimately reducing global inequalities.
title: The technological-financial-military linkage and the reproduction of inequality between countries

abstract: This paper examines the long-term impact of a randomized experiment offering intensive mentoring to adolescent students. In the short term, the program reduced school dropout by 40%. By linking the experimental data to administrative records, the impact can be assessed up to 13 years after the start of the program. We find that, in the long run, the program increased schooling while reducing suspicion of crime and decreasing family size. The positive schooling effects are concentrated among high-risk students, who also appear to earn higher wages. On the other hand, the program has no clear impact on the outcomes of low-risk students.
title: Long-run impacts of school-based mentoring for at-risk youth: evidence from a randomized field experiment

abstract: We study whether embedding a redistribution opportunity in political competition alters political ambition and narrows the gender gap in willingness to run for office. Existing evidence indicates that women are more inequality-averse and less likely to enter competitive settings, but perhaps more responsive to redistributive incentives. We test whether redesigning competitive political environments to include a redistributive opportunity, more specifically the option to transfer money to the lowest earner, can mitigate gender disparities in candidate entry. We conducted a laboratory experiment with 320 participants from the University of Alabama and Loyola Marymount University using a within-subject design. We find that the Redistribute-to-Lowest treatment increases willingness to run for both women and men by nearly 5%, but does not reduce the gender gap in political ambition: women report 17.6% lower willingness to run than men. We also find a negative correlation between willingness to run and giving, revealing a paradox: those most inclined to help others are often the least likely to seek positions that would allow them to do so.
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
title: The puzzle of political ambition and prosociality

abstract: The occurrence of bond defaults threatens the stability of supply chains. Vertical common ownership helps alleviate vertical conflicts between enterprises and tackle issues arising from incomplete contracts, thus potentially lowering the bond credit risk faced by upstream and downstream firms. Based on a sample of China A-share listed companies from 2010 to 2023, this study empirically examines how vertical common ownership affects the credit spreads of bonds issued by upstream and downstream firms. The results show that when institutional investors hold shares in both a focal firm and its upstream or downstream partners simultaneously, the credit spreads on bonds of those upstream and downstream firms are effectively narrowed. This effect grows stronger as the ownership proportion increases. Overall, this research offers practical insights for improving supply chain resilience and fostering the high-quality growth of the bond market.

abstract: Kremer, Willis, and You (2022) report that over six decades richer countries lost their growth advantage. Acemoglu and Molina (2022) and Pesaran and Smith (2026) reply that such regressions cannot measure catch-up when countries head toward different moving destinations. We nest both in one model. The movement survives across countries: the between-country income gradient of growth fell abruptly in the decade from 2003. Nulls with fixed destinations, or built to Pesaran and Smith’s specification, do not reproduce it. Only a lower bound on convergence speed survives: the within-country bias cannot be separated from the estimate.
title: "Eppur si muove": Convergence Within and Between Countries

abstract: This paper evaluates the temporary reduction in energy taxes implemented by the German government between 1 June and 31 August 2022. Measured against the delivered cost of importing the same fuel from the Amsterdam–Rotterdam–Antwerp (ARA) region, German wholesale prices net of tax rose by 5–6 (gasoline) and nearly 4 (diesel) cents per liter during the cut, corresponding to measured pass-through of 83% and 73%. The two numbers have different economic interpretations. We separate them using heating oil, the same middle distillate as diesel but with no tax cut. We find that the diesel wedge reflects the 2022 gasoil supply shock rather than seller conduct. Therefore the diesel tax cut was passed through in full. The gasoline wedge, however, is genuine retention of about 382 million Euro, a sixth of the gasoline subsidy. We also find that retention is largest where regional buyers are affluent and locally captive. Mobile bulk-buying haulage, in contrast, disciplines diesel pricing. Lastly, we show that pass-through is enforced by the threat of imports. This arbitrage ceiling was suspended when historically low Rhine water levels physically rationed inland supply.
title: The rise of refinery margins: The case of the energy tax cut in Germany

abstract: Firms often install pollution-abatement equipment but operate it below full capacity to save on running costs. We study how this gap between installed and used abatement shapes environmental regulation. In a model where firms first invest in abatement, a regulator then sets an emission fee, and firms finally choose how much capacity to use, partial usage emerges when installation is inexpensive but operation is costly. A regulator who anticipates partial usage should set a stricter fee; one who assumes full usage sets fees that are too lax and lets emissions rise. Partial usage is more likely in concentrated industries, so investment subsidies that look green on paper can leave emissions unchanged once firms scale back usage. Recognizing that installed capacity is not the same as abatement delivered is essential for designing emission fees and green-investment subsidies that actually reduce pollution.
title: Idle abatement capacity: Usage costs and the design of emission fees

abstract: Large-scale solar installations support the transition to low-carbon electricity but also occupy land that provides wildlife habitat. We examine changes in bird observations following photovoltaic deployment in the United States using data from 2003 to 2021. A difference-in-differences analysis of eBird, a source of birdwatching records contributed by the public, finds a substantial decline in recorded bird counts following installation. The estimated decline is considerably smaller in the Breeding Bird Survey, a standardized monitoring program. Changes in land cover and differences in responses across bird species provide suggestive evidence consistent with habitat disruption. Our results inform the balance between solar energy expansion and habitat conservation.
journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

abstract: Informal institutions often persist even when governments expand formal alternatives. Evidence from Ghana’s rollout of land registration offices shows that improved access to statutory land institutions did not significantly increase the adoption of formal agricultural land rights. Instead, formalization appears to be constrained by village chiefs. To interpret these findings, we develop a model linking land markets to informal risk-sharing networks, in which chiefs’ power limits the take-up of formal land rights. While partial adoption of land rights improves consumption insurance and the efficiency of land reallocations, full formalization can unravel informal insurance networks. The persistence of informality may therefore reflect a rational response to the value of local cooperation.
title: The mystery of land rights: Explorations on informal institutions in Ghana

abstract: In one-shot delegation, a principal facing a possibly upward-biased agent caps action from above. Under repeated delegation, a biased agent gains more than an unbiased one from appearing unbiased, because that relaxes the future cap. When the agent cares enough about the future, both types are locked in a signaling race and pool at downward-distorted actions. The optimal early-period interval therefore imposes a binding lower bound despite the upward bias, while its cap is less restrictive than in the one-shot game. Both bounds relax as the agent values the future more. With a strong signaling motive, the floor is Pareto-improving.
title: Signaling in Repeated Delegation

abstract: This paper examines the process of dividing a fixed surplus as a multilateral bargaining game with costly recognition. We establish the existence of equilibrium and explore the roles of the institutional rules that govern this process. Specifically, we consider a design problem in which the designer maximizes a general objective function by determining both the voting rule—i.e., the minimum number of votes required to approve a proposal—and the mechanism for proposer recognition, modeled as a biased generalized lottery contest. We demonstrate that any feasible outcome regarding equilibrium efforts and recognition probabilities can be implemented using a rule that incorporates a dictatorial voting rule. In other words, the designer can maximize her interests by resolving the distributive process through a simple static biased contest.
title: Orchestrating the Distributive Process: Baron and Ferejohn Meet Tullock

abstract: We show that supply-side effects arising from the bond holdings of open-end mutual funds affect corporate credit risk. In our model, open-end funds are reluctant to roll over bonds with weak prospects, fearing future outflows. This lowers rollover prices, enhancing equityholders’ default incentives, and increases credit risk. Empirically, we find that in firms with weak prospects, fund holding shares increase CDS spreads, and more so when flows are more sensitive to performance. We provide direct evidence for the relevance of the rollover channel, use two quasi-experiments and an instrument to address endogeneity concerns, and rule out reverse causality via reaching-for-yield.
title: Bond funds and credit risk

abstract: The Critical Access Hospital (CAH) program, established under the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, provides cost-based Medicare reimbursement to small rural hospitals in exchange for limits on inpatient capacity and service scope. We estimate the effects of CAH designation on hospital finances, capacity, and organizational outcomes using a synthetic difference-in-differences design that exploits the staggered 1999–2002 rollout of state-level CAH availability. We find that CAH designation raises operating margins by three to four percentage points, with no change in liquidity or capital investment, as cost-based reimbursement sustains revenue while expenses fall with scale. Designation also reduces inpatient scale, with significant declines in total beds, obstetric capacity, and nursing staff. Emergency department visits also decline meaningfully, while outpatient volume is largely unchanged. At the same time, CAH designation reduces hospital closures, with no meaningful effect on mergers. These results point to a “survival versus scale” tradeoff across hospitals within a state, wherein designation-based subsidies avert closure for a small number of hospitals while inducing widespread inpatient downsizing among the many more hospitals that convert. Because converting hospitals shed more inpatient capacity than averted closures preserve, the program may reduce aggregate rural inpatient capacity even as it keeps hospitals open.
title: Survival versus scale: The effects of critical access hospital designation

abstract: In this paper, I model how climate risk disclosure impacts climate risk sharing among investors. I show that this disclosure can improve risk sharing by helping investors identify stocks that effectively hedge climate risk, and I analyze the disclosure’s impact on investors’ equilibrium portfolio choices. I then study firms’ voluntary disclosure incentives and analyze when disclosure mandates enhance risk sharing. Finally, I demonstrate that, by facilitating risk sharing, climate risk disclosure reduces the climate risk premium among stocks held by climate-focused investors. Hence, disclosure can lower the valuations of firms with low climate exposures and the overall market. (JEL: D82, D84, G12, G14)
title: Climate Risk Disclosure and Risk Sharing in Financial Markets

abstract: Preservation-led programs dominate the regeneration of heritage-industrial brownfields in Global South cities, overshadowing territorial assets, constraints, and demand. Few replicable, demand-first, multi-scale frameworks explain how post-industrial land-use changes can be derived in institutionally complex and economically stressed contexts. This research proposes a causal-asset framework based on sustainable urban livelihoods, asset-based community development, and system dynamics to study the role of assets, barriers, and feedback loops in determining adaptive reuse strategies. The framework is applied to the Ray Cement Factory, Tehran, Iran, a case rich in information combining national industrial heritage, long-term underuse, metropolitan accessibility, university assets, and reuse constraints. The methodology innovatively integrated three-scale asset inventory; purposive group model building; causal diagramming; and strategy derivation. The analysis reveals two interconnected negative dynamics due to the absence of innovative spatial infrastructure. One is a territorial deprivation trap characterized by skills deficits and suppressed entrepreneurship, and the other is an asset underutilization trap that leads to heritage deterioration and disinvestment. The breaking of this link can trigger two self-reinforcing structures, the Innovation Ecosystem Loop and the Heritage Identity Loop, that underpin precinct viability. This study contributes by deriving programming from diagnosed territorial demand. It operationalizes heritage-historical capital as a non-substitutable, stock-like category grounded in a national-first industrial identity. The findings indicate that asset-strategy coherence requires alignment at the metropolitan, immediate urban, and site levels. The framework helps planners connect heritage protection, economic activation, and policy coordination.
title: From territorial deprivation trap to innovation precinct: A causal-asset framework for industrial heritage brownfield land use change

abstract: An environmental limit, such as a carbon budget, changes the nature of economic growth, but does not preclude it. When atmospheric greenhouse gas levels reach a critical threshold, further economic growth requires a permanently expanding and resource-intensive mitigation effort. If too slow, technical progress in mitigation becomes a constraint and the ultimate determinant of economic growth. Secularly expanding GDP remains a durable feature of this class of economies and characterizes the social planner’s optimum under conditions of exogenous and directed technical change. In both cases, a binding environmental limit reduces the long-run rate of economic growth.
title: Economic Growth and Greenhouse Gas Mitigation at the Environmental Limit

abstract: Using a shift-share design that leverages the unanticipated Venezuelan migration crisis, I examine immigration’s impact on educational attainment in Ecuador. Immigration positively affects standardized test scores, consistent with greater effort among course takers aiming for college enrollment. Test scores show no significant effects on primary or middle schoolers. The effects lead to more college graduates and more high school dropouts, widening educational inequality. Student composition and the intensity of preparation for college admission among course takers explain the results.
title: Immigration, selection, and human capital: The Venezuelan inflow and educational pathways in Ecuador

abstract: This paper addresses two long-standing questions in the political economy of development: how the timing of industrialization affects the transition to democracy and how different social classes shape that transition. We develop a sequential game among landed elites, industrialists, and workers embedded in a growth model with endogenous industrialization. The model identifies a window of democratic opportunity during which the industrial class prefers democracy to industrial autocracy. Whether democracy occurs depends on two dimensions of workers’ de facto political power: their power against the landed class determines when industrialization occurs and when landed rule ends; their power against the industrial class determines when the democratic window closes. Later industrialization therefore makes democratization less likely but not impossible. A calibration to Great Britain and numerical exercises for early and late industrializers show that the revolt threat required to sustain democracy rises as industrialization is delayed. Faster technological growth advances political transitions but does not, by itself, determine whether democracy or industrial autocracy follows landed rule.
title: Industrialization, class conflict, and the closing window of democratic opportunity

abstract: This study examines optimal k -double auctions with ownership premia. We consider independent, uniformly distributed material values and an affine premium fixed across mechanisms. We show that k = 1 / 2 remains optimal if the premium is constant or included in welfare. On the other hand, if the premium increases with the seller’s material value and is excluded from welfare, the optimum becomes k < 1 / 2 . It generates fewer trades but higher expected material gains. The selected linear equilibrium attains the second-best for material gains among Bayesian incentive-compatible, interim individually rational, and ex-ante budget-balanced mechanisms.
title: Ownership premia and optimal k-double auctions

abstract: Forecasts of the effect of on jobs usually start from the tasks a machine can perform. Radiology, the medical specialty most exposed to AI, points to a different margin. This column uses US Medicare data for 2013–2024 to show that as AI tools spread, radiologists did not read more scans and the profession kept growing, but radiology work moved out of small local markets and into multi-state groups. The evidence fits a mechanism in which AI makes expert work done elsewhere easier to check. The costs of AI may fall less on occupations than on places.
title: AI and the geography of expert work: Evidence from radiology

abstract: A barrage of transportation disruptions has affected the global economy in recent years. This column examines how transportation bottlenecks interact with aggregate shocks, comparing the Commodity Supercycle of the 2000s and the post-pandemic Great Supply Chain Disruption. The spike in freight rates for dry bulk shipping in the former episode was due to scarce shipping capacity, while the latter stemmed from scarce port capacity. Shipping prices rise dramatically when transportation capacity is scarce, while port prices remain much more stable. The constraint matters: when ships are scarce, shipowners have strong incentives to order new vessels, but addressing port scarcity may require government intervention.
authors: Giulia Brancaccio, Myrto Kalouptsidi, Theodore Papageorgiou, Yixin Zhou

abstract: Rising temperatures are increasing residential electricity demand as households rely more on mechanical cooling in hot urban environments. In much of the energy and climate literature, higher electricity use under heat is treated as evidence of successful private adaptation and preserved thermal comfort. This paper shows why that inference can fail when comfort is unevenly experienced within the household. Using linked intra-household survey data and administrative electricity records from Singapore—a dense tropical city with near-universal electricity access—we examine whether electricity demand is associated with within-household differences in reported thermal comfort that may reflect heterogeneous thermal preferences. We measure within-household variation using individual reports of comfort in unconditioned (non–air-conditioned) indoor environments, which may reflect heterogeneous thermal preferences and tolerance as well as differences in exposure. Households with greater comfort dispersion consume significantly more electricity per capita, conditional on mean comfort, income, dwelling characteristics, appliance stock, ventilation practices, and cooling behaviours. A one-standard-deviation increase in comfort dispersion is associated with approximately 5.6% higher electricity consumption per capita. By contrast, the max–min comfort gap is not significantly associated with electricity use. A complementary diagnostic analysis finds no statistically significant association between higher electricity consumption and narrower within-household comfort gaps. Together, the results are consistent with heterogeneous thermal preferences creating coordination and allocation challenges in shared cooling decisions, while highlighting why aggregate electricity use alone cannot reveal how comfort is distributed among household members—with implications for residential energy-demand modelling and the assessment of heat adaptation.
title: Electricity demand without shared thermal comfort: Intra-household thermal preference heterogeneity under heat

abstract: Nonlinear real exchange rate models are typically based on the assumption of time-invariant market frictions. In this paper, we propose a time-varying-parameter smooth transition autoregressive model that facilitates inference on the evolution of market frictions and exchange rate volatility. Using a long-span monthly dataset on the dollar–sterling real exchange rate that covers more than two centuries, we estimate the model in a fully Bayesian framework via Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Our results provide evidence of long swings in the degree of market frictions over time. Furthermore, we show that real exchange rate volatility has exhibited large and persistent movements. These movements can be partially attributed to changes in the exchange rate regime. A generalized impulse response analysis indicates that the speed of real exchange rate adjustment to shocks varies substantially across historical periods. In a complementary exercise, we apply the model to dollar–sterling deviations from mint parity during the Classical Gold Standard and provide evidence of substantial time variation in market integration.
journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control
source_issue: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control
title: Drifting STAR: A Time-Varying Nonlinear Real Exchange Rate Analysis

abstract: In the late nineteenth century, Americans feared that crowded immigrant neighborhoods were spreading disease through industrial cities. We study this claim using newly constructed town-level panel data from Massachusetts, 1860 to 1915, a setting uniquely suited to this exercise because its early vital registration system allows consistent measurement of mortality before national registration became widespread. Using a shift-share instrumental variable strategy based on historical settlement patterns, we estimate the effect of local exposure to immigration on mortality. We find that increases in the foreign-born share significantly raised infant and child mortality, with the infant effect falling disproportionately on the post-neonatal period. Mechanical changes in the composition of births by parent nativity account for only a portion of the estimated effect, implying that the results are not driven primarily by higher mortality among immigrant births. Instead, the evidence is consistent with increased exposure to immigrants, communicable disease, and spillovers to children of native-born parents. These findings highlight immigration as one factor shaping the mortality transition in crowded high-mortality environments.
title: Immigration and child mortality during the Age of Mass Migration

abstract: Under the private-values assumption with possibly correlated types, I consider revenue maximization in multi-object auctions with each buyer having additive valuations and with fairly general feasibility constraints. After calculating buyers’ virtual valuation vectors using the revenue equivalence theorem, I identify an upper bound for the seller’s expected revenue obtainable among all Bayesian incentive compatible (random) mechanisms satisfying each buyer’s interim individual rationality. I introduce a multidimensional regularity condition under which I can construct a dominant-strategy incentive compatible (random) mechanism which maximizes the revenue. When the multidimensional regularity condition is violated, I develop an ironing procedure which allows me to construct such a mechanism. To derive those results, I show that ray monotonicity, which is seemingly weaker than monotonicity, is equivalent to dominant-strategy implementability under the appropriate conditions.
title: Multidimensional mechanism design and robust revenue maximization in multi-object auctions

abstract: Liberalization of temporary contracts has been a hallmark of labor market reforms during past decades. More recently, factors like the sovereign debt crisis induced the most indebted countries to enact unprecedented reductions of employment protection also on open-ended contracts. These policies are justified on the assumption that EPL hampers the allocation of workers to the jobs where they are most productive. How EPL affects the quality of matches, here measured in terms of (statistical) educational mismatch, is nonetheless an underexplored issue. We provide new evidence that exploits one of these recent reforms, enacted in Italy in 2012 against the background of austerity reforms. The results show that educational mismatches decreased. Moreover, the reduction in EPL favored labor reallocation. Eventually, it has also been followed by an increase in productivity, albeit small. While the results are consistent with the economic theory that informed deregulation, we highlight caveats and limitations.
title: Job Protection and Educational Mismatch: Evidence from an Italian Reform

abstract: Numeracy (defined as the ability to understand and use probabilistic and other numeric information) predicts large differences in financial outcomes, health status, subjective wellbeing, and decision processes. These effects are well-documented and some causal studies exist. However, objective numeracy alone is not enough to explain who benefits from behavioral interventions. Here, I introduce the Motivational Mind framework, which argues that numeric confidence (i.e., people's beliefs about their own mathematical ability) is a distinct construct that also interacts with objective numeracy to predict decision-making processes and outcomes. The framework builds on Kahneman's dual-process framework, while reconsidering the assumption of universality embedded in the heuristics-and-biases program. I propose that these two numeric competencies—objective numeracy and numeric confidence—together predict who shows which numeric biases and why. Outcome anomalies particularly concentrate in two counterintuitive cells: high-ability/low-confidence people who have skills that go unused, and high-confidence/low-ability individuals whose motivated engagement goes unsupported by skill. Three psychological mechanisms are consistent with what we know about these constructs: (1) the more numerate derive greater affective meaning from numeric comparisons, highlighting effects of the affect heuristic in the numeric domain; (2) numeric confidence drives persistence and deployment of ability; and (3) math-generated negative emotion leads lower-confidence people to undervalue numerically complex options. I then reframe four evidence-based interventions as mechanism-targeted strategies that predict differential individual-difference benefits. I close with a research agenda identifying critical gaps, including the need for heterogeneous treatment-effects tests in field settings and for more causal testing, especially with numeric confidence.
title: Tailoring Behavioral interventions: The roles of numeracy and the motivational mind

abstract: We study core-selecting auctions for double auctions that incorporate package bidding. Unlike in one-sided core-selecting auctions, the core may be empty in more general double auction settings, and truncation strategies need not be amongst a bidder’s best responses. Nevertheless, we establish the existence of a core-selecting auction in which every imputation in the core with respect to true preferences corresponds to a strong Nash equilibrium. Specifically, for any core imputation, there exists a profile of truncation strategies that constitutes a strong Nash equilibrium and induces precisely that imputation.
title: Strong Nash Equilibria of Core-Selecting Double Auctions

abstract: We study scoring procurement auctions with risk-neutral parties, quasi-linear payoffs, and quality costs partly sunk regardless of winning. Under the difference-score rule, we characterize in closed form the unique symmetric pure-strategy equilibrium with scores decreasing in type and bounded price bids. We then derive the procurer-optimal scoring rule. With power-form costs, a higher all-pay share lowers quality, total surplus, and supplier payoffs but ambiguously affects procurer payoff. Reimbursing losers’ all-pay quality costs increases quality and supplier payoffs but reduces total surplus and procurer payoff. The optimal score subtracts price from a quality index that underweights quality relative to the procurer’s payoff function. Under a weakly convex inverse reversed hazard rate, its marginal quality weight weakly increases with the all-pay share and number of suppliers. Our equilibrium approach extends to minimum-score constraints, multidimensional quality bids, and general scoring rules.
title: All-Pay Quality-Bids in Score Procurement Auctions

abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments in the euro area sharply increased spending while the European Central Bank eased financing conditions. We use this episode to assess how such a concerted monetary–fiscal stimulus redistributes welfare across age cohorts. Our assessment involves not only the income side of household balance sheets (mainly direct effects of transfers) but also the more obscure financing side that, to a substantial degree, occurred via indirect effects (with a prominent role of the inflation tax). Using a quantitative life-cycle model and assuming that the deficit was only partly funded through future taxes, we document that young households benefited from the stimulus, whereas middle-aged and older households mainly paid the bill. Crucially, most of the welfare redistribution was due to indirect effects related to macroeconomic adjustment that resulted from the stimulus. As a consequence, even though all age cohorts received significant transfers, the welfare of some actually decreased.
title: For whom the bill tolls: Redistributive consequences of a monetary–fiscal stimulus

abstract: We study the trade-off between spending reductions and bureaucratic costs associated with managed care tools in healthcare. We use random assignment to Medicare Part D plans to study this trade-off for prior authorization restrictions. Prior authorization reduces a drug’s utilization by 27%. Half of marginal beneficiaries are diverted to another related drug, while the other half are diverted to no drug. Eliminating prior authorization would increase drug spending by $100 per beneficiary-year (4% of drug spending), while reducing paperwork costs by $10.
title: Rationing Medicine Through Bureaucracy: Authorization Restrictions in Medicare

abstract: We study how firm-level technological change a↵ects skill demand and wage inequality in the presence of imperfect competition on the labour market. We show that skill-biased technological change raises both firms’ skill ratio and skill premiums, whereas alternative shocks cannot generate this pattern. Combining employer-employee data with innovation surveys from Norway and Hungary, we document that firms adopting new technologies increase both their skill ratios and skill premiums. A calibrated model implies that technological change increased the aggregate college wage premium by 3.2% (5.3%) in Norway (Hungary) over 10 years, highlighting the important role of firm-level innovation in shaping inequality.
title: Firm-level Technological Change and Skill Demand

abstract: Most social media users have encountered toxic content online, but there is scarce evidence of how it impacts engagement. In a pre-registered browser extension field experiment, we randomly hid toxic content on Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube for six weeks. Lowering exposure to toxicity (i) reduced time spent, content consumption, advertising impressions; (ii) reduced the toxicity of user-generated content; and (iii) led to substitution to nontreated social media platforms. A complementary survey experiment shows toxic content triggers users’ curiosity, increasing engagement. Taken together, our results suggest that platforms face a trade-off between curbing toxicity and increasing engagement.
title: Toxic Content and User Engagement on Social Media: Evidence from a Field Experiment

abstract: U.S. employers and the federal government devote the equivalent of 1.5% of GDP annually toward promoting defined contribution (DC) retirement savings. Using a new employer-employee linked dataset covering millions of Americans, we show that tax and employer matching incentives disproportionately benefit White and Asian workers compared to their similar-income Hispanic, Black, and American Indian or Alaska Native coworkers. Similarly, these incentives disproportionately benefit those with richer parents compared to those from lower-income families. Breaking the link between contribution choices and saving subsidies through revenue-neutral reforms could close up to one-third of the DC wealth gaps by race and parental income.
title: Who Benefits from Retirement Saving Incentives in the U.S.? Evidence on Gaps in Retirement Wealth Accumulation by Race and Parental Income
